summary: Defines version 2 of the protocol operations for SNMP, including the syntax and the procedures for sending, receiving and processing SNMP PDUs. It is the part of the framework that describes the actual requests and responses between managers and agents. It replaces RFC 1905.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3416 defines the requests and notifications used by SNMP management systems. It explains what a device returns when a manager reads or changes information.

subtitle: The message formats and procedures for SNMP requests, responses, changes, and notifications.

tldr.problem: SNMP managers and managed devices need shared rules for reading and changing management information and reporting events.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3416 defines SNMP protocol data units and processing rules for retrieval requests, bulk retrieval, setting values, responses, traps, and informs.
tldr.outcome: It is Internet Standard STD 62 and obsoletes RFC 1905. The RFC says its many changes from RFC 1905 do not change the protocol itself.

sections.title: Where These Operations Fit
sections.content:
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) framework includes architecture, a way to describe managed objects, message protocols, protocol operations, and applications. RFC 3416 defines the protocol operations: the rules for sending, receiving, and processing protocol data units (PDUs).

Managed objects are described in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). SNMP entities acting as managers send operations, while entities acting as agents respond or originate notifications. The document prefers an unreliable datagram service, with each message contained in one transport datagram; UDP is the preferred mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP operations are the messages a management system uses to access information on a device. This RFC defines how the device processes those messages and replies.

sections.title: PDU Structure and Variable Bindings
sections.content:
An SNMP PDU is defined using ASN.1. Most PDU types share fields for a request identifier, error status, error index, and variable bindings. A variable binding pairs a variable name with a value or an exception; the name is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER.

GetBulk uses fields named non-repeaters and max-repetitions in place of the error fields. A response copies the request identifier so the requesting application can associate the response with its request. The PDU definitions include error statuses and retrieval exceptions such as noSuchObject, noSuchInstance, and endOfMibView.
sections.plainLanguage: Each SNMP message identifies the request and carries a list of named values. The response uses the request identifier to show which request it answers.

sections.title: Reading Values and Walking Tables
sections.content:
GetRequest asks for values with exact names. If a name does not identify an accessible object, the response distinguishes an unknown object from a missing instance. GetNextRequest returns the first accessible variable whose name follows each requested name in lexicographic order.

Repeated GetNext requests let a manager walk through a table by asking for the next name after the most recently returned one. GetBulkRequest retrieves successors for several names in fewer exchanges. Its non-repeaters and max-repetitions fields set the requested number of bindings, but the response may be shorter because of message-size limits, the end of the available data, or processing limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Get asks for named values, while GetNext asks for the next available name. Repeating GetNext lets a manager move through a table; GetBulk can request several results at once.

sections.title: Changing Values and Returning Responses
sections.content:
A SetRequest first checks whether every requested value can be assigned. If all checks pass, the assignments are made as if they happened together. If an assignment fails, the implementation undoes the other assignments and reports commitFailed; if it cannot undo them all, it reports undoFailed.

A response carries an error status and, when appropriate, an error index identifying the failed binding. A trap reports an event without confirmation. An inform reports an event and expects a response, although the RFC notes that delivery is not guaranteed.
sections.plainLanguage: Before changing several values, the device checks that every change is allowed. A trap does not request confirmation, while an inform does.

sections.title: Security and Status Today
sections.content:
The protocol operations defined here do not provide a secure environment on their own. Even a protected network does not decide which users may access management information. The RFC recommends using the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model, with configuration that limits access to legitimate users.

RFC 3416 is Internet Standard STD 62 and obsoletes RFC 1905. Its changes section describes clarifications and editorial updates, and says that most protocol-related edits do not affect the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: These message rules do not control who may read or change device information. Access protection must be provided and configured through the SNMP security framework.
